title: The Fourth Revision on the Whiteboard
teaser: On moving day, the apartment building’s only elevator stops working, and the truck permit expires at eleven. Ajie knows how to get large furniture around the landings, Mei knows when the stairs must remain open for residents, and Lin Lan needs her belongings upstairs, while the property manager who formally controls the common areas cannot get back in time.
paragraphs: At 9:05, when a yellow OUT OF SERVICE notice appeared on the elevator doors, Lin Lan’s furniture was already taking up half the lobby. The moving company’s temporary parking permit ended at eleven. Twelve boxes, a sofa, and a tall cabinet that could not be dismantled were still downstairs. Normally, Ajie handled the moving route and the safety of large items, the property manager decided whether common fixtures could be moved, and the cleaner, Mei, used the stairs according to her own cleaning schedule. Now the manager was dealing with a leak in another building and could not return for a while. Ajie took a tape measure upstairs and came back to write on the small whiteboard beside the elevator: “Third-floor landing: 76 cm. Cabinet can pass.”

For efficiency, the next step should have been to carry the small items up continuously, then move the cabinet while the stairwell was clear. Mei returned with her cleaning cart, saw the board, and added two fixed routines she dealt with every day: “9:55 — resident on third floor comes down with walker; 10:30 — rubbish collection on second floor.” Lin Lan then checked with the residents who had to leave that morning and added “10:20 — stroller from fourth floor” on the right. Ajie erased half of his original “all boxes first” and replaced it with: “small items before 9:40; keep passage clear at 9:55; cabinet at 10:05.” No one took over anyone else’s job, but one person’s information had already changed the sequence for the other two.

At 10:05, the cabinet reached the second-floor landing. Ajie judged that the safest turn required standing it upright, with two movers occupying the entire third-floor landing for about three minutes. Mei, however, could see that the elderly resident from the third floor had not yet gone back upstairs; the walker was still by the door. Moving immediately would save the most time, but it would block the building’s only passage. Lin Lan went downstairs to confirm that the resident was resting in the ground-floor seating area and would not be returning immediately. Mei pushed her cleaning cart back into the storage room. Only then did Ajie cross out the time after “cabinet” on the board and rewrite it as “10:08–10:11 — third-floor landing occupied.” The cabinet followed his technical plan, but when it moved was not determined by dimensions alone.

At 10:20, the fourth-floor resident came down with the stroller exactly as noted. The cabinet was already through, and Ajie was ready to start on the sofa. Lin Lan called for the movers to wait two minutes, following the whiteboard, while Mei kept a courier who had just arrived in the lobby. Once the stroller had passed, Ajie measured the sofa arm again and suggested removing a wall lamp at the second-floor turn, which would eliminate one rotation. It was the easiest solution from a moving perspective, and Lin Lan had already taken out a screwdriver when Mei pointed to the property label beside the lamp. All three stopped. None of them had authority over a common fixture.

They did not leave the sofa until the afternoon. Ajie used thicker protective blankets and rotated it from the other side. Lin Lan checked again that no resident had to come down before 10:30. Mei directed the rubbish collection staff to the basement entrance first, leaving a full flight of stairs for the sofa. At 10:27, it scraped past the turn against the padding. The whiteboard was now on its fourth version: the measurements remained, the access times had been revised three times, and a new line at the bottom read, “Do not remove common fixtures.” The person who moved the next step forward kept changing, but every change depended on someone else’s information or boundary.

At 11:10, the property manager returned, added the repair work-order number to the yellow notice, and confirmed that the elevator would not be back before the afternoon. He inspected the access route and resumed responsibility for the equipment room, fire requirements, and common fixtures; no one had gained those powers during the morning. Lin Lan was about to wipe the whiteboard clean when Mei said there was another delivery in the afternoon and the access rules could stay. Ajie had already driven the truck away. The original “76 cm” and the residents’ times were erased. What remained was “confirm access first,” “occupy only one flight of stairs at a time,” “do not remove common fixtures,” and three shades of handwriting.
explanation: Leadership can be observed from different perspectives. A position perspective focuses on formal roles, responsibilities, and authority. A relational or influence perspective asks whose judgment or information actually changes other people’s actions in a specific interaction. A process perspective looks at how several people jointly form the next step as the task keeps changing. These perspectives do not replace one another, and they do not imply that formal authority disappears. They make different sources of leadership activity visible within the same episode of collaboration.
mapping: The property manager is absent, yet no one is free to decide about the wall lamp, equipment room, or fire requirements → From a position perspective, formal authority persists; temporary collaboration does not automatically absorb the powers of a role.

After Mei provides the fixed access schedule, Ajie changes the moving sequence; after Lin Lan confirms the resident’s status, the cabinet can move → A relational or influence perspective asks who, in a specific interaction, actually changes another person’s next action.

The cabinet, stroller, sofa, and rubbish collection successively become the immediate constraint, so the person proposing the next step changes with the problem → Leadership activity does not settle permanently on Ajie simply because he has the most moving expertise.

The whiteboard is rewritten repeatedly by all three, and every version incorporates another person’s information or boundary → A process perspective sees not one temporary leader’s plan, but coordination being formed step by step through interaction.
boundary: Understanding leadership through multiple perspectives does not mean that “everyone is a formal leader,” nor does it mean that collaboration can replace positions, responsibilities, or authority. High-risk decisions, legal accountability, people management, and control over resources may still have to remain with designated roles. The framework mainly helps reveal different sources of leadership activity within the same situation; it does not by itself show that distributed coordination is always more effective than centralized direction.
reflection: If the morning were recorded only as “the property manager was absent, so Ajie took charge of the move,” what on the whiteboard would disappear even though it actually changed what people did?
